cases.abstract: LoRA reduces trainable parameter counts, but its differences from full fine-tuning concern how updates are expressed as well as their rank. In VL-BART, decomposing weight columns into magnitude and direction reveals positively coupled changes under LoRA, whereas full fine-tuning exhibits a negative correlation. Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) normalizes pretrained weights plus a low-rank update, then scales each column with an independently learned magnitude. This separates scale adaptation from the directional changes represented by the low-rank factors. Adapted weights can be merged before inference without additional adapter latency. Across eight commonsense reasoning tasks, LLaMA-7B average accuracy rises from 74.7% for the published LoRA baseline to 78.4% for DoRA, with 0.83% and 0.84% trainable parameters, respectively, under the reference configuration with learning-rate adjustment. Halving DoRA's rank yields 77.5% accuracy with 0.43% trainable parameters. In a separate LLaMA-7B ablation, detaching the normalization denominator reduces training memory by 24.4% with a 0.2-percentage-point accuracy decrease. Multimodal aggregate scores also improve over LoRA, but video performance remains below full fine-tuning. Separating magnitude from direction thus offers a useful alternative to increasing the low-rank parameter budget.
cases.methods: An additive low-rank update must express both directional and scale changes in pretrained weight columns. DoRA gives rescaling its own parameter: each adapted column is a learned magnitude multiplied by the unit direction of W0 + BA, where W0 is frozen and A and B are trainable low-rank factors. Initial magnitudes equal the pretrained column norms, and BA starts at zero, preserving the original weights at initialization. Column normalization removes scale from the quantity controlled by the low-rank factors, allowing the magnitude vector to adjust it separately. Differentiating through normalization rescales the weight gradient and removes its component parallel to the current direction. The evaluated implementation instead recomputes the denominator in each forward pass but detaches it during backpropagation. This reduces the gradient graph's memory cost and retains magnitude learning, while using a scaled rather than projected directional gradient. The distinction separates the analyzed optimization geometry from the memory-saving implementation.
cases.results: DoRA's gains do not require a larger trainable parameter budget than LoRA's. Half-rank DoRA reaches 77.5% average commonsense accuracy on LLaMA-7B with 0.43% trainable parameters, compared with the published LoRA baseline's 74.7% with 0.83%. On LLaMA-13B, the corresponding accuracies are 80.8% and 80.5%, with 0.35% and 0.67% trainable parameters. These comparisons use the reference configuration with learning-rate adjustment, supporting better evaluated accuracy at smaller budgets without isolating decomposition as the sole cause. The VL-BART query-weight analysis provides a complementary check: magnitude-direction correlations are -0.31 for DoRA, -0.62 for full fine-tuning, and 0.83 for LoRA. This supports the intended change in update pattern, but that resemblance does not eliminate the performance gap. The video-task aggregate increases from LoRA's 83.5 to DoRA's 85.4, below full fine-tuning's 87.5, with a substantial remaining deficit on YC2C captioning. LLaVA visual instruction tuning similarly improves the aggregate score while losing to LoRA on VQAv2 and VQAT. The evidence favors more economical adaptation, not uniform task superiority.
cases.notes: Final text check: the abstract links independent column scaling to smaller-budget accuracy (Eq. 5; Table 1); Methods distinguishes normalization's full derivative from denominator detachment (Eqs. 6, 11); Results contrasts update-pattern resemblance with the video performance gap (Fig. 2; Table 3). Table 1 supports a 0.3-point half-rank LLaMA-13B gain, not the narrative's 1 point. Table 7 reports VL-BART scores 77.3 and 77.4 rather than exact equality. Keep the separate LLaMA-7B figures of 78.4 (Table 1) and 78.1 (Tables 6/7) unpooled pending clarification. Multimodal aggregates combine task-specific metrics and are not uniform accuracy percentages.

cases.abstract: Optimizer statistics can be compressed without restricting model weights to a fixed low-rank parameterization. GaLore projects gradients into a compact subspace, updates optimizer moments there, and maps the processed update back to the full weight matrix. Periodically refreshing the projection lets accumulated updates span different directions, addressing the limitation of learning within one fixed subspace. Conditional analysis establishes contraction of projected gradients with fixed projections under structured-gradient and curvature assumptions; the refreshed Adam implementation is evaluated empirically. In one untuned C4 pretraining comparison over 19.7 billion tokens on 64 A100 GPUs, 8-bit GaLore reaches LLaMA-7B validation perplexity of 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam. Separately, combining projection with 8-bit optimizer states and per-layer updates reduces the measured 7B training footprint to 22.0 GB at a small per-device token batch, without checkpointing or offloading. Per-layer updates save memory by avoiding storage of all weight gradients until backpropagation ends. GLUE fine-tuning scores remain near full fine-tuning, with small aggregate gains over LoRA. Lower measured throughput on the 1B model shows that the contribution is reduced memory pressure with largely preserved model quality, rather than faster training.
cases.methods: GaLore compresses the optimizer's representation of an update while leaving the weight matrix itself full-sized. For an m-by-n matrix with m <= n, the leading r left singular vectors of the current gradient form a projector P. The compressed gradient P^T G has r-by-n dimensions, so Adam stores its two moment arrays in that smaller space. The processed update is scaled, multiplied by P, and added directly to the original weights. Periodic singular-value decomposition refreshes P, allowing successive updates to leave the initial subspace rather than enforcing a fixed low-rank weight factorization. The supporting theorem concerns a narrower operation: with fixed projections, structured Lipschitz gradient components, bounded weights, no adaptive regularization, and sufficient projected curvature relative to component variation, the projected gradient contracts toward zero. This guarantees progress within the selected subspace, not convergence of periodically refreshed Adam to a full-space optimum. The refresh rule addresses subspace coverage empirically rather than inheriting that guarantee.
cases.results: At 1B parameters on C4, GaLore reaches validation perplexity of 15.64, close to full-rank Adam's 15.56 and lower than LoRA's 19.21 and ReLoRA's 18.33. Estimated weight-plus-optimizer memory is 4.38 GB, versus 7.80 GB for full-rank Adam and 6.17 GB for either adapter method; these estimates exclude activations and stored gradients. The comparison matches low-rank methods' ranks and learning-rate tuning budgets, with no full-rank warmup for ReLoRA. The contrast shows that, in this setup, reducing optimizer memory need not incur the larger perplexity penalties observed for adapter training. The single untuned 7B trial gives perplexity 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam on 64 A100 GPUs. The separate 22.0 GB measurement instead establishes memory feasibility for a small token batch, not completion of that pretraining run on one consumer GPU. Memory savings also carry a throughput cost: in matching 1B configurations at a 256-token batch, 8-bit GaLore processes 1019.63 tokens per second versus 1205.31 for 8-bit Adam. Preserving quality with less memory is the supported tradeoff.
cases.notes: Final text check: the abstract connects compact optimizer states and immediate layer updates to memory savings (Secs. 4.2-4.3, 5.5); Methods separates fixed-subspace contraction from refreshed Adam (Theorem 3.8); Results tests the memory-quality tradeoff against full-rank and adapter baselines (Tables 2, 3, 11). Estimated memory excludes activations and stored gradients; measured footprints include them. The 7B convergence trial used 64 A100 GPUs, unlike the small-batch single-device memory measurement. Smaller-model token budgets disagree between Tables 2 and 5, so they remain omitted. Throughput uses the matching Layer Wise 4 rows; clarify that field and the narrative's 17% overhead before broader efficiency claims.
